messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 27
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Journalist
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 64

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Trauma-Related Events: Trauma-related events, Public Transport: Bus riding, Male Presence: Being alone with men
  Maladaptive Strategies: Self-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what I have done wrong, Suppress Anger: never allow myself to feel or express anger, Undereating: I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping
  Threat: Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe, Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
  Memory: Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
  Negative Appraisals: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you, Mistrust: People can't be trusted, Inadequacy: I am inadequate

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Bao, a 27-year-old journalist, presents as articulate and composed, yet a deep exhaustion is evident in the set of his shoulders. The events that brought him to therapy occurred eight months ago, but for Bao, they have never truly ended. The trauma was an assault by his then-partner, a man whose volatility had been escalating for months. The final night began with a tense, quiet bus ride home from a friend's dinner. Bao remembers the feeling of the worn vinyl seat under his hands, the dread coiling in his stomach with every stop, knowing an argument was inevitable. The explosion happened just after they got off the bus, on the dimly lit street leading to their apartment. An accusation, a shove, and then a flurry of blows that left Bao on the cold pavement, a sharp, radiating pain in his ribs and a profound sense of shock.

In the months that followed, the world began to shrink. The bus became an impossible space; the squeal of air brakes or the rumble of an engine outside his newsroom window is enough to make his heart pound. He now takes expensive ride-shares or walks, adding an hour to his commute and significant strain to his finances. As a journalist, his work requires him to meet and interview people, often one-on-one. He now finds any meeting where he is alone with a man to be an exercise in controlled panic. He focuses on the exit, maps the distance to the door, and can barely retain the details of the conversation, convinced that you can never truly know who might harm you. This has made his work feel precarious, his once-sharp interview skills blunted by overwhelming fear. His editor has commented on the declining quality of his recent pieces.

The memory of the assault is not a coherent narrative he can recall at will; it is a sensory ambush. A story on the news about a local dispute can trigger it, and suddenly he is no longer in his apartment but back on that street. The memory feels intensely present, as if it is happening right now, complete with the phantom ache blooming in his side, a somatic echo of the real impact. The wave of shame and terror that accompanies it is so overwhelming that he has to physically stop what he is doing, often retreating to the bathroom to grip the sink until the world solidifies around him again.

At night, sleep offers little respite. He frequently wakes in a cold sweat, heart racing, and feels compelled to check the locks on the doors and windows, peering through the blinds into the empty street below. His new partner, Minh, is gentle and reassuring, but Bao finds that even when Minh tells him he is safe, the words feel hollow. He has come to believe that people simply can't be trusted, that a calm surface can hide anything. This conviction plays out in agonizing ways; if Minh is ten minutes late coming home from work, Bao’s mind doesn’t conjure images of traffic but of betrayal or disaster. He has learned to smother any flicker of his own anger, viewing it as a dangerous, volatile force that must be suppressed at all costs.

This vigilance is fueled by a relentless internal monologue of self-blame. He spends hours ruminating on what he must have done wrong to provoke the attack, convinced that he is fundamentally inadequate. This belief manifests in a quiet, punishing form of control: restricting his food. Some days he eats very little, the feeling of hunger a familiar, grounding distraction from the emotional chaos. He came to therapy after a weekend away with Minh, a trip that was meant to be restorative but was instead marred by Bao’s constant anxiety and inability to relax. He saw the hurt and confusion in Minh’s eyes and realised he was destroying the first safe relationship he had known. What frightens him most is the thought that he is permanently broken, but what he hopes for is to one day feel safe in his own body, in his own home, again.
